column2: Elbows about 90° at the keyboard, shoulders relaxed
Adjust the desk or chair height; consider a keyboard tray.
Mouse at the same level as the keyboard and close to it
Move the mouse right next to the keyboard; a compact (no number pad) keyboard reduces reaching.
Wrists straight, palms not resting on a hard edge
Use the wrist rest only while pausing; fold in the keyboard feet.
Handset not clamped between neck and shoulder during calls
A short break or change of position every 30–60 minutes
Set a reminder; break up static sitting with standing work and short walks.
Frequently used items within arm’s reach
Move the phone, documents and materials to where they can be reached without stretching.
Enough legroom, nothing under the desk
Remove boxes and cables from under the desk.
Bring the load closer to the body: remove obstacles, make the box pull towards the worker, use smaller packaging.
Bring the start height closer to waist level (≈75 cm): use a pallet raiser or shelf instead of picking from the floor.
Lower the start height below the shoulder; reduce picks from high shelves.
Shorten the vertical travel: bring the start and destination heights closer together.
Remove trunk twisting: put the pick and place points in the same direction or add a turntable between them.
Reduce lifting frequency or duration: job rotation, breaks, slowing the flow, or automation.
Improve the coupling: crates with handles, cut-out handholds or non-slip gloves.
Good: crate with handles or an easy-to-grip object
Fair: no handle, but fingers can wrap 90°
Poor: large, slippery, irregularly shaped object
Up to 1 hour (followed by at least the same time of light work)
Check screen or workpiece height with RULA (neck score) and the office checklist.
Look at the REBA/RULA upper-arm score and reach distances; check force frequency with HAL.
Check REBA/RULA trunk and neck scores; in the office, check the chair and screen.
Check force and repetition with the Strain Index and HAL, and forearm posture with RULA.
Assess repetitive work with the Strain Index, HAL TLV and the RULA wrist score.
Check lifting and carrying with NIOSH (CLI for mixed lifting) and KIM, and trunk bending with REBA.
Check the seating set-up (office checklist) and the REBA leg score.
Check work requiring squatting and kneeling with REBA/OWAS; check the working height.
Assess prolonged standing, flooring and footwear; check leg postures with OWAS.

Revised NIOSH lifting equation (1991). Calculates the recommended weight limit (RWL) and lifting index (LI) for smooth, balanced two-handed lifting/lowering tasks. Take the measurements at the start of the lift. If there are mixed lifts with different loads or heights, use the “NIOSH composite” form.
Horizontal distance between the midpoint of the ankles and the midpoint of the hands. Below 25 counts as 25; above 63 the RWL drops to zero.
V · Hand height from the floor
The best value is 75 cm (waist height). Above 175 the RWL drops to zero.
Difference between the start and destination hand heights. Below 25 counts as 25.
How far to the side of the body front the load is taken. Above 135° the RWL drops to zero.
The multipliers are fine; the problem is the weight. Split the load or use a mechanical aid.
One multiplier is zero: the measurements are outside the equation’s valid range.

Composite Lifting Index (CLI). For jobs where the same worker does lifts of different weight, height or frequency together (palletising, different shelf levels). Enter the measurements for each sub-task; tasks are ranked by single task lifting index (STLI) and the contribution of the others is added via the total frequency.
H, V, D, A: cm and degrees, as defined in the NIOSH form. F: lifts per minute for that task.
Enter load and frequency for at least one task.
Total lifting frequency is high: share out the tasks and reduce total repetition with rotation or mechanical aids.

Key Indicator Method (BAuA 2001 version). Scores the total load of lifting, holding or carrying repeated during the day. Also suitable for carrying and holding tasks that NIOSH does not cover. If there are different loads or postures, open a separate record for each.
Load score tables differ by sex.
The weight actually borne by the worker. Part of the load when tipping or dragging; roughly half in a two-person carry.
1 · Trunk upright, not twisted; load close to the body
2 · Slight forward bend or twist; load close or at medium distance
4 · Deep bend or bend+twist; load far away or above the shoulder
8 · Deep bend+twist, load far away; squatting, kneeling, unstable posture
0 · Good: enough space, level floor, good lighting, good grip
1 · Restricted movement space or unfavourable conditions (uneven floor etc.)
2 · Space very restricted and/or the load’s centre of gravity unstable
Reduce or split the load; use a lifting aid, trolley or conveyor.
Bring the pick/place height to waist level, bring the load closer to the body, remove twisting.
Widen the movement space, level the floor, use packaging that keeps the load balanced.
Reduce daily repetitions or distance: job rotation, bulk transport aids, a shorter layout.
Overload possible for less resilient people; work redesign is useful for them.
Overload possible for people of normal resilience too; work redesign is recommended.
Overload is likely; work redesign is needed.
Thresholds: under 10 low · 10–24 increased · 25–49 highly increased · 50+ high
Moore and Garg Strain Index (1995). Estimates the risk of hand-wrist-elbow disorders in repetitive hand and wrist work (assembly, packing, cutting, tightening). Assess each hand separately.
Light: barely noticeable, no clear effort
Hard: obvious effort, no change in facial expression
Near maximal: shoulder or trunk also used
Based on the observer’s rating or the worker’s Borg CR-10 answer.
Total time force is applied in a cycle ÷ cycle time.
Very good / good: neutral or near neutral
Fair: noticeable but not extreme deviation
Very bad: near the end of range
Very fast: barely or not able to keep up
Reduce the force required: tool maintenance, sharp blades, powered tools, lighter parts.
Shorten forceful holding: fixture, vice, tool balancer.
Reduce repetitions: split the job, rotation, automation.
Tools and layout that keep the wrist straight: bent-handle tool, tilt or rotate the workpiece.
Review line speed and pace pressure; add buffer stock.
Reduce the daily time spent on this task with rotation.
Increased risk of disorders; improvement recommended.
Associated with disorders; the job should be redesigned.
Thresholds: 3 or below safe · 3–5 uncertain · 5–7 probably hazardous · above 7 hazardous

ACGIH hand activity threshold limit value. Assesses the hand activity level (HAL, 0–10) together with the highest force in the job (normalised peak force, NPF, 0–10) and compares them with the threshold limit value (TLV) and action limit (AL). Developed for mono-task hand work lasting 4 hours or more a day. You can rate HAL by observation or calculate it from frequency and duty cycle.
Calculate from frequency and duty cycle
Number of movements in which the hand applies noticeable force.
Percentage of the cycle during which force is applied.
0 · Hand idle most of the time, no regular exertions
2 · Consistent, conspicuous long pauses or very slow motions
4 · Slow steady motion; frequent brief pauses
8 · Rapid steady motion; very infrequent pauses
10 · Rapid steady motion; difficulty keeping up
Ratio of the highest force in the job to the person’s maximum force in that posture (0–10). Without measurement, the worker’s or observer’s 0–10 rating.
Reduce movement frequency or force duration: split the job, automate, share between both hands, rotate.
Lower the force required: tool maintenance, powered tools, better handles, looser part tolerances.
General controls and monitoring (training, surveillance, complaint follow-up) recommended.
Exposure should be brought below the TLV with job-specific controls.

Checklist for desk and computer work. Not a scored scientific method; a compliance check based on common ergonomics guidelines. Mark each item Yes / No / Not applicable; every “No” produces a recommendation.

Work surface height calculator. The recommended height depends on elbow height and the type of work: slightly above the elbow for precision work, slightly below for light work, lower still for heavy work. Enter the current height to see the difference.
Precision work: fine assembly, high visual attention
Heavy work: pressing, cutting, heavy parts
How will you enter elbow height?
Standing elbow height is taken as about 0.63 × stature. You can add 2–3 cm for shoes.
Arm at the side, elbow bent at 90°, from the floor to the underside of the elbow. Sitting: measure while the person sits on an adjusted chair.
For precision work the height of the workpiece, for heavy work the height where the hand works. Leave empty to get a recommendation only.
Measure the elbow height or enter the stature.
If several people use the station, a height-adjustable bench or a personal platform is the best solution.
Enter the current height and I’ll compare.
Raise the surface: adjustable legs, risers; or lift the workpiece with a fixture. A low surface leads to bending forward.
Lower the surface or give the worker a platform (it must cover the whole movement area). A high surface leads to raised shoulders.
Current height is within the recommended range.
